utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to welcome all the people in the courtroom and without further ado I'm going to give the floor to the registrar for the IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Nermin Malovic. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 435; the list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number 436; the list submitted by 2D IC 437 shall be given Exhibit number; and the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 438.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have the blinds lowered and the witness introduced into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Would you please stand up. Could you tell me your name and surname. Do you hear what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear it. It's just that my headphones are not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, tell me your name, surname and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Mustafa Hadrovic. I was born on the 15th of August, 1945 in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I used to be a car mechanic, and lately I've been working in car inspection, technical car inspection, and I'm now retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you testified before a national or international court before on events in your country or is it the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a witness in my country about the abused that I suffered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before which court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The District Court in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You can sit down now. Just a few brief explanations. You will be questioned by the Prosecution first. The Trial Chamber decided to give the Prosecution two hours for the examination-in-chief, not a minute longer. Two hours. After that stage, the Defence will also have two hours to question you in the course of cross-examination. The Judges you see before you can intervene at any time and ask you questions. Your testimony will be over tomorrow at any rate. If you have whatever problem or feel whatever discomfort during this hearing, do not hesitate to let us know. If you do not understand a question, please ask the person who is asking the question to repeat it and make it clearer. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to now give the floor to the Prosecution for the commencement of their examination-in-chief, which is beginning now at 1750 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. First of all, good afternoon, Your Honours, and everybody present in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Good afternoon, yes, Witness, Mr. Hadrovic. I've got some questions to you, and let's start with very short part of my examination-in-chief. That's the event when you were mobilised into the Mostar CSB or security services centre. Is it really that you were mobilised to that centre?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. I was mobilised on the 19th of September, 1991, at the centre of public security in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Could you explain the Judges just very briefly what does this centre mean? What kind of agency was it? Was it a military agency or a civilian agency?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: It was a civilian service, a civilian agency, because in the system as it was then I had served in the army, and then I joined the reserve force of the police. I signed up on the 19th of September, 1991. It was the civilian sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Just as the active-duty policemen who worked at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: -- was it an overall body for the whole Bosnia and Herzegovina? I mean, newly created Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time. I mean, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was an overall body for the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have your -- the highest command in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, but all organisations, each in their own town, had their own police stations. Of course Sarajevo was the capital, and it was the top level from which everything went down along the chain of hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you use the coat of arms of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What kind of uniform were you using, wearing, at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: In those first days we wore the same uniforms as active-duty policemen. It was still the time of Tito's Yugoslavia. But later we got new uniforms of a different colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did it have any insignia? I mean the uniform you had.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: The first day when we put on that uniform there was just an inscription, "Policija," "police," and we wore that until the new year. After the new year we started receiving those new uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Was it a BiH uniform, Bosnia and Herzegovina uniform with the relevant insignia?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We had insignia of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and inside it was written "Police," "Policija."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And who was your highest superior in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Those first days in Mostar when I joined the police force, the chief of police was Viktor Stojkic, and Safet Memic was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Where did you have your headquarters in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: The command was in Mostar where you can see the police station standing to date, close to the Vranica building. I am not sure about the names any more because the street names have changed, and I really can't find my way around them any more, but the building is still standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: But at that time, what was the name of the street? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: It's close to Stjepana Radica Street. Then you go towards Splitska street. You could access it from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. No need. Witness, due to the restrictions of -- on time, I will skip the period of war on Yugoslavia, and the only question I will ask you, did you keep to be a mixed body at the end of the war against Yugoslavia in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which Yugoslavia is the gentleman referring to, keeping in mind the time, the period of time of the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1991, 1992. Just two -- 1992, more or less that period of time, because we started in 1991. It's quite clear what period of time I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand this question, and I can give you the following answer: When the war began, we were all together, Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs. Up to a point when a water tank exploded in Mostar near the North Camp. From that time on, all Serb policemen with some very few individual exceptions withdrew and were no longer in the station with us. According to our assignments, the main police station was near Vranica, and mine was at the intersection towards Semovac bridge. Croats and Muslims were there together, and my commander was Camil Basic. So until that water tank exploded, we were together, and then we split and only Muslims and Croats remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, after the war, beginning as of summer 1992, what were your daily duties as a police officer in Mostar? Did you have any specific area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: No, no particular duties. But since I knew the town well and I was born there in Donja Mahala --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] To avoid further confusion in the cross-examination, on the same line raised by Mr. Karnavas, we are talking now about the war that began in 1992, and then it ended. Which war are we talking about? Where it ended? Did it end in the area -- in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina? I think there will be complete confusion. I think our learned friend meant to say the war against Serbs in Mostar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You really have to be more specific. The Judges did understand, but maybe Defence counsel did not. So make it more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. I'll be very specific. I mean the war activities in the Mostar area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: In the Mostar area where you were working, in the adjacent area, just the period of 1992. That was the essence of my question. I'm not going further for reasons already well-known here.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: I understand the question perfectly, and I gave a perfectly good answer. Until that water tank exploded we were all together. And when the water tank exploded, Bosniaks and Croats remained together in the same stations, whereas the Serbs withdrew to the other side of the Neretva River, started setting up their own check-points, and real clashes, skirmishes began causing deaths and injuries. All that went on until they withdrew in June when Muslims and Croats crossed the Neretva River. By that time Serbs had already withdrawn towards Podvelezje and started targeting Mostar from that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: I can explain all that because I personally lived through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary now, but if there are any further questions during the cross-examination or examination by the Judges, perhaps they will ask you. My question was: Did you have any particular assignments? What were your daily duties from the period of time when we are talking now, June 1992, and further?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: We all got some assignments. One of the assignments was to watch over bridges, to take care that they are not destroyed or blown up. Since I knew Donja Mahala well because I was born there, we saw Hasan Brkic bridge, the Lucki bridge, and we guarded all of them, but what happened later was not prevented, and I will explain that later. I had no particular, no special assignments; the same kind of work as all the other policemen. Yes, occasionally I did get some assignments, but I can tell you about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what -- what was happening in your police body shortly after the war, 1992? I mean now July and further, autumn 1993 -- 1992. Did you keep to be a united force again as before the war with the Yugoslavia and shortly after the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: After the crossing of the Neretva River in July conflicts already started within the police force. It was over the display of state emblems on the building of the MUP. When those emblems were put up, rallies occurred and an armed conflict was barely avoided that day. The next day the symbol of Bosnia-Herzegovina was removed and replaced by the symbol of the HVO. Individual policemen were then disarmed, including the chief of the shift, who was Camil Basic at the time, and I was there that morning to report before going to Lucki bridge. I saw that something was wrong, and I headed towards Mostar Hotel. There I found my superiors, Safet Memic, Ramo Maslesa, and all the others including Sehic and Mrs. Nadja Kalesic and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. And just explain to the Judges. You mentioned the location Mostar Hotel. What did you have at the Mostar Hotel at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Since we had no place there in our location, we moved to the Mostar Hotel which was by that time already damaged by shells. We all sat there together with our superiors, and that's where we received our orders. Those policemen who came with the chief and the others were there, and then I joined them too. It was the police station for Bosniaks at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: But did you continue wearing your own uniform, I mean with the Bosnia and Herzegovina insignia? What kind of uniform were wearing the Croats? Members of the police, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: We, too, wore whatever we could lay our hands on, but before the conflict I received -- we received uniforms from the Croatian Defence Council, and we kept our insignia of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was the only legal and recognised state, after all. However, at that time our partners did not wear the same insignia. They wore HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And when did this mixed police cease to exist? In your understanding and observations.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: It ceased to operate already in September, October. The relations were not good any more, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Which year do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: 1992 and 1993, because after the crossing of the Neretva, we already saw some complications and disagreements with Croatia and members of the HVO as policemen. And it was the same thing with the army. Internal conflicts began within the forces, and one side started disarming the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: My question is: Did you have a separate command at that time already? When did it appear first, this separate command? For one, let's say police faction, and for the other one.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: They all had their own commands by that time. The HVO had their own command, and the BH insignia was worn by our force, and we received our assignments and orders from our superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And who became your superior?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Safet Memic became may superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And let's -- okay, let's now move to April 1993. How did it come about that you lost Mostar Hotel as one of your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Since the Croatian Defence Council demanded that we move from Mostar Hotel to avoid conflict, because we were very close, we moved to the Partizan Cinema Hall. It's on Santiceva street. And that's where we all moved. And there were members of the army there together with us, members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: You also mentioned just some minutes ago that a matter of -- your special concerns or concern were the bridges in Mostar. Were the bridges left untouched by the Serbs when they were leaving the area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: When the Serbs left, crossed over to the other side, there were exchanges of fire but not a single bridge was destroyed by the Serbs. I can prove that. Because at that time I passed across all the bridges, and I can mention some members of the HVO and who are still friends with me today who told me openly, "Watch out for your bridges." I don't know how, but I know that all the bridges that were guarded by the army and the police remained untouched. And then the moving out from Luka began, and all the bridges were destroyed. I personally watched over Lucki bridge and Hasan Brkic bridge. We had our booths there. I never saw, and other people can confirm this, I never observed anyone from the Serb army approaching those bridges.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Battalion came to help us guard the bridges. However, I cannot understand some things to this day. Whenever somebody came to replace us in guarding the bridge, that bridge was destroyed a couple of days later. At Lucki bridge, one of my colleagues was killed by a sniper from the Serb side who was shooting from Sehovina and the thoroughfare which is still called Marsal Tito Street today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, my question what about the old bridge? Was it also under protection of your forces?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the only one that wasn't destroyed then. Only the aviators' bridge was destroyed at that time. The Serbs had withdrawn and left some of their men there who got killed. I learned that from commander Arif Pasalic and his associates who are still alive, unlike Arif.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, just -- I'm asking you, did you have any particular assignments with respect to the old bridge?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did have an assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What kind of assignment?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: When we finished with the Serbs, when Serbs retreated to Nevesinje, I received orders to be at the old bridge to take care that there should be no looting of property and that the businesses not be harassed. And I can say that all the businesses from the tinsmith to the tobacco factory were indeed all right. I can vouch for that. Unfortunately, great looting began later that could not be stopped. Passenger cars and trucks went back and forth taking property out across the bridges as well, but I didn't let any of those vehicles cross over my bridge. And I can guarantee with my word of honour that nobody was allowed to take a needle across the bridge. We checked all the vehicles, and we checked some vehicles, asking drivers where the property came from that they were carrying, and they said, "From my home," and we knew exactly they were not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, that's enough. My question is: And where was that stolen property taken to while you were on duty on the old bridge, let's say?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you just one example. The people who were at the North Camp, HVO was stationed there, and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was to the south. The northern part had all the compressors emptied overnight. Workshops looked like an atomic bomb hit them. Everything disappeared. The only thing that couldn't be carried away, and that's still there today, are heavy machines. Only they could not be carried away. We caught a lot of them, but it was all useless. Even if you reported them, nobody had the time to pursue it. And I can guarantee that the old bridge was the only one that I and my colleagues did not allow anyone to take anything across. My colleague was Jure Markic, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... little bit, little bit. Who were the people who were committing such kind of lootings?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you straight away. Among those people were all the criminals, first and foremost. Criminals do not abide by faith or nationality. I caught them from all groups, but I caught them most from the HVO, and they said, "The Chetniks will move in again and they will take it all away. Anyway, it's better that we take it." However, we members of the army, we had had no where to store it, to keep it. We already had very little room. If we had tried to guard some of the vehicles such as brand new mini-vans and everything, we couldn't. All that went to Siroki Brijeg for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a brief question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, sometimes you say "I," sometimes you say "we," but who was in charge of securing that bridge? What was the size of that force, police or military, because you said on the other side there were members of the HVO. So what was that force securing the bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the outset we were 15 on the old bridge, and we switched, took turns to secure the movement of troops from one bank to the other. Everything went according to plan. There were only members of one ethnic group at that point. Later, in order to establish peace and harmony, from six to seven members of the HVO arrived, and they were with us for a while but not for long. I don't know what the purpose of that was, why they were there, but we watched over that bridge, we members of the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And I want to clarify another question. While talking about the bridges, you mentioned the period of time when most of the bridges were blown up. Could you explain what particular period of time or range of time did you mean in your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Before we crossed the Neretva, and the Neretva was crossed in June --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Which year? What year? For the record.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: 1992 we crossed the Neretva. At the time, or up until then, not a single bridge had been destroyed while the Serbs were on the left bank. After their withdrawal and while we controlled the bridges, we controlled them together, afterwards the 4th Battalion arrived and the bridges began to snap. And I was at the Lucki bridge when a good friend of mine was killed, Sacir Sacovic, from a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: He was shot by a sniper. But the bridges, I can never prove that they destroyed the bridges, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, let's -- let's stop at the moment. Let's stop at the moment now. You -- you mentioned the 4th Battalion. Which was -- 4th Battalion did you mean? To what military faction did it belong?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: It was the 4th Battalion of the Croatian Defence Council, and after us they came to guard the bridges, and among them was a neighbour of mine. He lives in Italy now. I'm sorry, but he said he would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: We made a lot of mistakes. We made a great mistake in letting anybody else guard the bridges except for the BH army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, let's pass to another set of questions now. Were you at some point arrested in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was arrested on the 11th of April. I was coming back from the old bridge, because I was still down there. I reached the health centre, and I was stopped there by a patrol. I saw that something was wrong. On the one side there were BH army members, on the other side members of the HVO. I was stopped at that point by Dzidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And who was Dzidic? Please explain to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the Croatian Defence Council. We knew each other. And he simply asked me, "Mujo, where are you off to, and what weapons are you carrying?" I didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I had an old jacket, I think the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He looked at me and he said, "Sit down." And I set off home on a motorbike. I reached the Djacki Dom in Stjepan Radic Street and the corner of Splitska Street and an HVO member pushed me down, took away my automatic rifle, took my -- MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] We have an error in the transcript. On page 86 [Realtime transcript read in error "84"], line 12, it says that Zeljko Dzidic said to the witness, "sit down." He didn't say sit down. He said, "happy journey," according to the witness. Sretno.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He said Sretno or, "Happy journey, you can go." He didn't say, "Sit down." And then I went home on a motor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Just one question to clarify. You mentioned that -- a Mr. Dzidic. Do you remember his full name and his particular position that he was holding at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: To tell you quite honestly, Dzidic was in the position of the military police, and I can say that I can't accuse him of anything. I cooperated with him nicely. He didn't mistreat me or abuse me in any way, and I can say that quite frankly. I gave my statement, so I can say that. But on my way home, and that was a different period of time, from the crossroads at Semovac to my road I was on the motorbike. Everybody knows what that place is called, Trafikana, Djacki Dom, I was knocked down at that corner and junction and taken to the faculty. At the faculty --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Stop --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, please. I think I must correct the correction. Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic pointed out to a mistake on page 84, line 12. You find that on page 48, line 17, and you were referring, I think, to page 86 and not to page 84. So it's -- there's a misunderstanding, and it gets difficult if this is -- goes on from mistake to mistake. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Just -- Witness, I would like to hear from you the date when you were arrested. So far you have not mentioned it. Do you remember the date when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: I was arrested --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I was taken to the faculty.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult for me to say what I experienced and what terrible abuse and mistreatment I suffered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What date was that, Witness? What date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 11th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What date were you arrested, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 11th of April. That's when they took me to the faculty building, and I know the building by heart. I know the precise room they took me to and where they tied me to, to the radiator. A young man was sitting there, Alikafic, Mirzo's son. And there was a picture of Ante Pavelic. I asked him for a sip of water and Cipra who was an active-duty policeman, he can bear that out. He lives in Mostar to this day and I met him, and it was very difficult for him when he knew what happened to me. I was taken to Heliodrom from the faculty building. Pero Marjanovic, Ante Buhovac, Tomic waited for me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: We have not clarified all the questions relevant to faculty building. First of all, could you explain the Judges what faculty building did you mean? Its full name.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: The faculty -- the infamous faculty, if I can put it that way. It used to be a JNA barracks. That's where they took me to. They beat me there, beat me and beat me, and I still suffer from that. And then they tied me to the radiator.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Poryvaev. In the indictment the mistreatment at the it mechanical engineering faculty started on the 9th of May. This witness is speaking on the 11th of April. That is not in the indictment. So ask your questions focusing on the indictment, exclusively on the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suggest that I'm asking questions relevant to the indictment, relevant to paragraph 17 and 39, talking about places where the people were detained and tortured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but people were tortured at precise dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, let's go further to Heliodrom. By whom were you taken to Heliodrom? Was it on the same day, on the 11th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: I was taken by a member of the Croatian Defence Council. He was a big man, and he limped on one leg. But I know that -- I know who took me over there. Marjanovic took me over there. Ante Buhovac did, or Ante Buhovac. The warden of the prison was Bozo. Then there was Daka Tomic and the other policeman, Puce, Ivica Delic nicknamed Krca, and many others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] Witness, answer in a precise way. You have an extraordinary memory, so focus. Focus on the questions you're being asked, because you have the tendency to elaborate and drift off into other areas and subjects. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise for interrupting my colleague here, but I believe, Mr. President, you had issued a ruling and that is for the gentleman to stick to the events in the indictment. That's how I took it. The gentleman did make his record, but then he proceeded to back to the same area in which you cautioned him to move. So was that a ruling? If not, I apologise for the interruption. If it was indeed a ruling, then I suggest that my learned colleague proceed and abide by the Court's rulings as we all must do in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You should tackle what is in the indictment, and just that. So you have to rein your witness in, because he has the tendency to speak of other topics. What we're interested in is what happened to him with respect to what is contained in the indictment, the charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Again, in our paragraph 17 and 39 of the indictment, we're talking about various places of detention which existed before the 9th of May, 1993. Exactly Heliodrom existed as from September 1992. That was the purpose of my question, just to prove that Heliodrom existed and functioned in April 1993. That was the purpose of my question. And the next question was who was running Heliodrom. That was the purpose of my exercise. But if you consider it unnecessary, I might skip it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ask him the question then. Ask him the question to see who was in charge and running Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know any of the people who took you to Heliodrom from the mechanical faculty?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: The young man who took me, I didn't know him. He was a large guy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poryvaev, you're not asking the right questions. We want to know who was running Heliodrom and you asked him who took him to Heliodrom. Now, in April 1993, who, according to you, was in charge and running Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian Defence Council. Because we had had no access down there at all, because they started incarcerating Bosniaks in Heliodrom already at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, Heliodrom is defined in paragraph 119. It's a problem of context. You say it's the HVO, but who was the person in charge of Heliodrom, the director or whatever you'd like to call him, but the person in charge, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Praljak Josip, and then there was Ante Smiljanic. Then there was Bozo -- what's his name? Stanko Bozic. He was the warden, because I had a number of contacts with him and talks with him while I was at Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know to what military unit or organisation they belonged? I mean the persons mentioned by -- by yourself just a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: They were members of the Croatian Defence Council, because there wasn't a single Bosniak there. No Bosniak policemen at Heliodrom at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: You mentioned Bosnian policemen. Did you see any other policemen in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: No. Well, there was another army there, other units there, other soldiers from -- well, the Gromovi, for example. Tuta's men, the Convicts Battalion. Many units were at the Heliodrom; that was the sort of base. But apart from these units there were no other units except the Croatian Defence Council and members of the other units, the Convicts Battalion and the other units of the Croatian Defence Council and the Croatian army. If I need to prove that later on, they were all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, when you are saying about Gromovi unit as deployed at Heliodrom complex, which unit do you mean? Was it a unit familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you. Those units -- well, there were many units down there, but I didn't know about that. I didn't know them, and later on -- well, until I was in prison myself. But I did know the Convicts Battalion and Tuta's men and many other people who were there then dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Gromovi, was it an HVO unit?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, they had the patches, the red insignia, red patches. Whether it was the Croatian army or whether it was -- well, later on I learnt that they were Croatian soldiers, these Gromovi. They were terrible. They destroyed everything in their path. And I know all the Convicts Battalions and the ones that took me and mistreated me and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When were you released from Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: On the 17th. I was released on the 17th. That was when I first entered prison. And I reported to the station at the Partizan Cinema Hall. The doctors examined me there. I had terrible scars on me, and I still have them to this day. It was a very difficult thing. When somebody hits you with his fist and I hit the radiator, then of course I had injuries to my head and the doctors gave me certificates, but they stayed in the Vranica building and I wasn't able to access any of that. I did manage to get some documents, but I can prove this. I took them with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you notice any changes in Heliodrom after April 1993, when you came back from Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did notice a lot of changes. There were big changes because big units began to gather there. I couldn't say which units I didn't see. I saw all sorts of units. I saw units of the Croatian army, and I know the men who were there. Later on, if I need to say this, these people were in prison with me later on too. Many units and many heavy weapons and tanks and mortars and many other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: While talking about military units, weapons, equipment, artillery, which army do you mean or armies do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: I mean the armies of the Croatian Defence Council and the Croatian army that took part there, too, and I can prove that. And the other armies, other soldiers, well, there were many units. All the convict whatsits, Tuta's men, the Gromovi, all the patches and insignia. I know some of my friends went to work for the Croatian army and made bunkers. I will tell you about that in due course, when I was arrested for the second time and taken to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, my question was, okay, you saw a lot of weapons, soldiers, units. Did ABiH undertake any measures at this same time to get ready for some possible actions from the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm totally lost as to the time frame that we're dealing with now, and I wonder if counsel could clarify that perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I asked the witness about the period after April 1993 when he was released from -- from Heliodrom, and he explained that that period of time when he got freedom he saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, with all --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Such things --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With all due respect that wasn't quite clear. It appeared, at least from my understanding of the transcript, that when he went back, he was asked, did he see any changes. That means after he was released and he went back. I assumed the gentleman was talking about May when he went back there. But if we could just get a chronological, you know, testimony, it would be nice. It would be easy for both of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poryvaev, to avoid the Defence getting up on their feet and Judges asking questions, because when Judges ask a question it's because you fail to ask them, try and be very specific in your questions. We need chronology so that everybody can find their way. We know that he -- that we're dealing with the 17th of April, so go on from there, because after the 17th of April we come to the 9th of May. So be specific in your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now, just I will ask you about May. Did you participate in any high-level meetings in Mostar at the beginning of May 1993 devoted to the situation in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, I did attend. I did participate on the 8th in what was previously the JNA centre, Dom JNA. That was Arif Pasalic was there, Memic, and the others. They were sort of factors at the time. When I left Heliodrom I had lost quite a lot of weight and didn't do any work, but I can say here and now that had the BH army prepared anything or wanted to organise anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: -- they wouldn't have --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: -- I must stop you now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Poryvaev. Once the witness said that he participated in the meeting you should have asked him the question of what was the object of the meeting, because if you don't step in the witness goes on rambling and tells us more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the transcript I wanted to intervene with -- in line 9 on page 95, the witness said in enumerating those present that there was Arif Pasalic, Hujdur Memic, and others. "Hujdur" has been left out. We know that. We have documents, so Hujdur and Orucevica. And Orucevica was omitted too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poryvaev, ask the witness the question about what the object of the meeting was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Witness. That was the question I wanted to ask you. What were the items on the agenda, if any, specific questions, well-prepared and well-organised meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, Your Honours. There was no organisation. Quite simply they asked themselves what was happening in Hum and the other hills, the concentration of certain units there. I asked myself the same question. I asked at that meeting. I said, "Gentlemen, you're probably sleeping in your own homes. I sleep in the Djacki Dom." They said there's no problem. I said, "Are we preparing any actions?" Nobody was preparing anything. I can say that with absolute certainty. Had there been any preparation for anything, then quite certainly I wouldn't have been taken to prison and solitary confinement cells down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to clarify. The people who were present at the meeting, because you had just intervention of one of the Defence counsel on that, please could you clear up again who was present at that meeting and was it held in the morning, in the afternoon, or in the evening on the 9th -- 8th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He never stated the date.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. He never stated the date. Let's get a -- let's get a step-by-step process. When was the meeting? Why was he there? In what capacity was he there? Now you've just given him the date. If we can just get it one step at a time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: It's in the transcript. The date is 8th of May, and he explained in what capacity he was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, just something to do with the transcript. A very important sentence by the witness was not recorded in the transcript, and it should have been in lines 10, 11, 12, on page 96. The witness said that he told his colleagues at the meeting that he sleeps near the Djacki Dom and then asks them the question, "Can they sleep peacefully?" Now, this question, "Can they sleep peacefully?", was not recorded that way, but their answer was recorded that they can because nobody was preparing anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, Mr. Poryvaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, were you at home on the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What did you observe from your home and where is your -- or was your apartment located in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: My apartment is exactly at the crossroads of the avenue, Stjepan Radic number 35. The building is -- it has a yard, and Slavko Njegus had the opposite apartment. He was a Serb. He was taken away, taken off just like I was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What did you observe? What was happening in the neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, as I was very ill, on the 9th of May they woke me up at 15 to 5.00. Strong explosions woke me up at quarter to 5.00, and in my yard, in the courtyard, there were these infamous mortars, the MGs or whatever, and the other weapons. And when I saw what was happening, I almost died on the spot, and my neighbour came to help me. Srecko did. And he said, "Stand firm. Keep -- don't be afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness, my question. You said that, "They woke me up." What or whom do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: The strong explosions. I was woken by the strong explosions and the attacks on Vranica building. They were terrible explosions, strong detonations, and I thought the whole town was toppling, and you could see that on the film, on the footage, on the photographs. You can could see where the Vranica building was, where the BH army members were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: From where were those shellings coming?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: The shells were coming from -- well, as I live in Stjepan Radic Street there was the Autoprevoz company, the transport company, or, rather, the bus-stop. Actually, their buses. Their buses belonging to their company parked there. And then there was the Djacki Dom and Velez stadium, and I with my very own eyes looked out of the window, that's how my building is positioned, and with my own eyes I could see the mortars, all types of mortars, the MGs, and the weapons and the soldiers that were there. All sorts of soldiers, all armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Stop. My question -- one moment. From what side? What factions were the shelling coming?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Shells were coming from the left side to the right side where Vranica was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I mean military faction.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: It's from Velez, the Velez stadium. The military might of the Croatian Defence Council. They were attacking the Vranica building then. And, Your Honours, I can also say that in those three days until Vranica fell I experienced some very difficult moments because I was very ill and I cannot forget what happened to the present day and I watched it all from my building, from my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness. I will ask you this question. Don't make comments unless you are asked. You said that you saw various soldiers in the area of the Vranica building. Could you clarify: What soldiers did you see? From what military units or military, let's say, factions?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA HADROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that, Your Honours. They were units of the Croatian Defence Council, the military police. Tuta's fighters. Stela's fighters. I can't explain all this to you. Perhaps you won't even understand me when I say, but the whole town knows this. It was a terrible sight to behold. There was not a single unit that wasn't represented there. There were lots of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poryvaev, move on. We've already seen a video of the Vranica building attack, so we have a lot of the elements that we know about. So try and move ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But perhaps if you allow one question. Did you identify soldiers that came from the Croat army? From the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you straight away. There was Splico, nicknamed Splico. He was in prison later with me, this man Splico, and he took part in the attack on Vranica. And his eight friends. And I can prove that, Your Honour, certainly I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Poryvaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Why are you talking about this man? Do you know that he belonged to any particular unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Poryvaev. It's five to 7.00. We're going to stop there because it has been brought to my attention that the witness needs to take some medicine at 7.00. So by the time he goes back to his hotel that will be that. We'll have to do this tomorrow as well because he has to take medicine at a precise time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask you something. Since I have until 8.30 to take my tablets, I can continue because I don't want to leave the building when I'm so hot and have to go into the cooler air. I know my body well, and 14 days ago I had an operation to -- so I can take the tablets by 8.30. That's the outside limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you've told us that you had an operation quite recently, it would be better to be prudent. And as it's almost 7.00, we are going to adjourn. You will be back here at 2.15 for the sitting then. Mr. Registrar, may we have the time calculations? I would like to tell the Prosecution that there are a lot of documents. Perhaps you should move on to present the documents, if you want to do so, and don't leave it to the last minute. You have used about 50 minutes it appears, so you have exactly one hour and 10 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try to do my examination-in-chief on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have overnight to arrange your examination, to be as effective as possible, and I invite all of us to come back tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of February, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.58 p.m.,
